question: Wireless earbuds can stutter when one particular kitchen appliance is running nearby, because it uses the same radio frequency. Which appliance?
source_excerpt: Both devices use the 2.4 GHz band; a microwave's magnetron produces high-power waves in that range, and tiny amounts of radio waves escape during cooking.

extra.why_interesting: Many people have heard their earbuds crackle in the kitchen without knowing why. The answer connects two everyday gadgets nobody thinks of as related, and the 'kitchen appliance' plus 'radio waves' clues make it something players can work out.
extra.verification_notes: Microwave ovens operate in the 2.4 GHz band shared with Bluetooth and are well documented as causing earbud dropouts; no newer development changes this (https://www.slashgear.com/1768736/why-headphones-cut-out-when-using-microwave).

explanation: Both Bluetooth and microwave ovens work around 2.4 gigahertz. A little leakage from the oven is enough to drown out your music for a moment.

question: The Bluetooth symbol on your phone is really two letters from an ancient alphabet, the initials of a Viking king the technology is named after. Which alphabet?
source_excerpt: bind rune merging the Younger Futhark runes Hagall (H) and Bjarkan (B), Harald Bluetooth's initials

extra.why_interesting: Everyone has seen the angular Bluetooth symbol thousands of times and assumes it's an abstract tech squiggle. It is actually two Viking letters fused together. The Viking-king foothold lets the player work out 'runes' on their own.
extra.verification_notes: The Bluetooth SIG confirms the logo is a bind rune of Hagall and Bjarkan, Harald Bluetooth's initials, so 'Runes' is correct (https://www.bluetooth.com/about-us/bluetooth-origin/).

explanation: It merges the runes for H and B, for Harald Bluetooth, the Danish king who united Scandinavian tribes. The engineers liked the idea of a technology that unites devices.
